strengths: Theoretically sound contribution: Theorem 1 elegantly derives optimal shrinkage coefficient without distributional assumptions; clever leave-one-out construction preserves gradient unbiasedness despite using biased baseline

Comprehensive experimental validation: Consistent improvements across 4 domains (math, logic, multimodal, RLHF), multiple models (1.5B-8B), diverse rollout counts (2/4/8), with direct variance verification showing 11-67% reduction
Practical utility: Zero hyperparameters, simple implementation (20 lines of code), minimal computational overhead, immediate drop-in replacement for existing RLVR methods
Thorough robustness analysis: Systematic ablations on difficulty/semantic heterogeneity, extended training curves, ground-truth value function and policy gradient comparisons, 5-seed averaging

Excellent presentation: Clear motivation grounded in RLVR's unique low-rollout regime, intuitive bias-variance exposition, well-organized experiments with comprehensive appendices including implementation details
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap on assumptions: Theorem 1 optimizes MSE but classical James-Stein guarantees require Gaussianity; RLVR rewards are typically binary/non-Gaussian. Authors acknowledge but dismiss briefly without analyzing impact of this violation

Modest improvement magnitudes: Pass@1 gains typically 2-5% (e.g., MATH500: 2.3%), consistent but incremental rather than transformative. Main paper lacks confidence intervals or statistical significance testing

Limited technical novelty: Core technique is classical James-Stein shrinkage (1950s-1960s); application to RLVR is novel but primarily engineering-focused. Leave-one-out solution, while clever, is relatively straightforward given RLOO precedent

Incomplete edge case and numerical stability analysis: When v̂_{-i} + ŝ_{-i} → 0, potential division issues not discussed. Boundary behavior when variance/dispersion approaches zero needs rigorous treatment. No minimum threshold guidance provided

Narrow experimental scope: Only tested with GRPO+RLOO setup; unclear if benefits generalize to other critic-free algorithms. Comparison against modified GRPO (without σ_i normalization), reducing direct comparability. No code repository mentioned; requires expensive hardware (GH200/H100) limiting reproducibility

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: identifies genuine challenge of accurate baseline estimation with limited rollouts (2-16) in RLVR

Solid theoretical contribution: Proposition 1 establishes unbiasedness, Proposition 2 derives optimal shrinkage coefficient, Theorem 1 extends to general case with leave-one-out construction maintaining unbiasedness
Practical implementation: simple method requiring ~20 lines of code, no hyperparameters, negligible computational overhead, easy drop-in replacement
Comprehensive empirical validation: consistent improvements across multiple domains (math, logic puzzles, multimodal, RLHF), model sizes (0.5B-8B), with 2-5% typical gains and up to 32% for RLHF
Direct variance evidence: Appendix B shows ground-truth baseline MSE reduction of 13.4-39.4% and policy gradient L2 norm reduction of 5.7-12.5%
Adaptive behavior: shrinkage coefficient λ̂ naturally adjusts—decreases with more rollouts and decays during training without manual tuning
Well-organized presentation: clear progression from policy gradient variance to baseline MSE to shrinkage principle, good balance of main text and appendices
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: applies classical James-Stein shrinkage (1956) to baseline estimation; while well-executed application, lacks fundamental theoretical innovation

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 derives optimal λ⋆ for population quantities (v2, s2) but practice uses plug-in estimates from limited data; no finite-sample analysis of how λ̂ estimation error propagates to policy gradient variance

Indirect connection to policy gradient variance: Theorem 1 optimizes baseline MSE rather than policy gradient variance directly; empirical variance improvements (Figure 8) are reassuring but not theoretically guaranteed

Incomplete method limitation analysis: minimal discussion of failure regimes (e.g., highly heterogeneous prompts), batch size dependence on shrinkage utility, or robustness to poor variance/bias estimates

Limited baseline comparisons: primarily compares against RLOO; Table 2 comparisons use single small model (0.5B) on GSM8k; no comparison with critic-based methods (PPO with learned value functions, SAC, etc.)
Modest empirical improvements: many results show 1-5% gains; lacking statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or variance/std dev across seeds despite using only 5 random seeds

Scope limitations: method specific to critic-free RLVR with batch structure; limited applicability to continuous RL or algorithms not using per-sample baselines; behavior under different reward distributions not thoroughly explored
Reproducibility concerns: many hyperparameters in Appendix D.5, computational cost unclear, large-scale experiments require significant compute access, some implementation details underspecified
